newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US, Britain claim Iraq ruined oil deal this month.
newsitem.headline: US, Britain claim Iraq ruined oil deal this month.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday that if Iraq had not sent its troops into the Kurdish north the oil-for-food deal could have been implemented in early September.

Edward Gnehm, the deputy U.S. representative, made the comment during a response to a U.N. General Assembly speech from Iraq's foreign minister Mohammad al-Sahaf, who accused the United States of delaying the plan for political reasons.

"The truth is that the secretariat of the United Nations had informed Iraq in late August that implementation ... could begin in the first week of September," said Gnehm in the first public confirmation that the oil deal apparently had been that close to implementation.

"By today's date, oil could well have been flowing and humanitarian goods already delivered (if) not for the action Iraq took in August 31. That is the only reason for the current delay in implementing the resolution" that sets out terms for the oil-for-food place," he added.

Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali put the plan on hold until he could be certain U.N. personnel in Iraq were safe following Iraq's offensive in the north to aid one Kurdish faction and the subsequent U.S. missile attack.

The oil-for-food deal would allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of crude to purchase food and other necessities for its people suffering under U.N. sanctions. The embargoes were imposed in August 1990 when Baghdad's troops invaded Kuwait.
Gnehm said that United States was in favour of implementing the plan "far more than the very well-fed Iraqi leadership."
But did not say when the plan could be implemented and U.S. officials in Washington have claim there will be a substantial delay.

British envoy Stephen Gommersall made a similar point in his comments to the assembly, saying that the plan "could have been operation even now, except for Iraqi government actions in the north of the country."

Gnehm also defended Boutros-Ghali against Iraqi newspaper criticism, one of the few times a senior U.S. official has done so since Washington earlier this year said it would veto his bid for re-election for not reforming the U.N. enough.

"We are disappointed that we did not hear from the foreign minister that he would stop punishing the secretary-general, who was again attacked viciously in the Iraqi press today, to change the administrative arrangements the secretariat has already prepared in order to implement 986," Gnehm said.

He was referring to an article in Babel, the newspaper owned by Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's son, Uday, which accused Boutros Boutros-Ghali of delaying the oil-for-food deal because he wanted to please the United States and further his chances for re-election.
